title: Zero-Knowledge Technology
tagline: Proving something is true without revealing why, and how it scales blockchains

modules.title: What is a zero-knowledge proof?
modules.summary: A zero-knowledge proof lets you convince someone a statement is true without showing them the secret behind it. Checking the proof is usually much easier than making it.
objectives: Explain the idea of proving without revealing
Name the two roles in a proof: prover and verifier
Give everyday examples of why this is useful

sections.heading: Proving without revealing
sections.body: Imagine proving you know a password without ever typing it where anyone can see. A zero-knowledge proof does this with math. You convince someone a statement is true, but they learn nothing else. The secret stays with you.

sections.heading: Prover and verifier
sections.body: There are two roles. The prover knows the secret and creates the proof. The verifier checks the proof and decides whether to accept it. In blockchains, the verifier is often a smart contract.

sections.heading: Checking is cheaper than doing
sections.body: Making a proof can take a lot of computing power. Checking it is usually fast and cheap. This gap is what makes zero-knowledge useful for blockchains. One party does the heavy work once, and everyone else can verify it quickly.

sections.heading: Two big uses
sections.body: The first use is privacy: proving a payment is valid without showing who paid whom. The second is scaling: proving that thousands of transactions were processed correctly with one small proof. Many projects use the same math for both.

concepts.definition: A proof that a statement is true which reveals nothing beyond that fact.
The party who knows the secret and creates the proof.
The party who checks the proof and accepts or rejects it.
The claim being proven, such as knowing a value that produces a given hash.

example.title: Proving you are over 18
example.body: A website needs to know you are an adult. Instead of uploading your ID with your full birth date and address, you share a proof that says only that you are over 18. The site can verify the proof, and it never sees your birth date.

modules.title: Completeness, soundness and zero-knowledge
modules.summary: Every zero-knowledge proof system must satisfy three properties. Understanding them tells you what a proof does and does not guarantee.
objectives: Explain the difference between interactive and non-interactive proofs
Explain what a circuit is in a proof system

sections.heading: Completeness
sections.body: If the statement is true and the prover is honest, the verifier will accept the proof. In short, true claims can always be proven. A system that sometimes rejected honest proofs would be useless.

sections.heading: Soundness
sections.body: If the statement is false, a cheating prover cannot convince the verifier, except with a tiny chance. This is what makes proofs trustworthy. A flaw in soundness would let someone prove things that are not true, such as a fake balance.

sections.heading: Zero-knowledge
sections.body: The verifier learns nothing except that the statement is true. The proof does not leak the secret or any part of it. Some systems used for scaling do not need this property, so they are better called validity proofs, even though people often still say ZK.

sections.heading: Interactive vs non-interactive
sections.body: Early proofs needed many rounds of back-and-forth questions between prover and verifier. Non-interactive proofs fit into a single message that anyone can check later. Blockchains need the non-interactive kind, because the proof is posted once and checked by many. To make a proof, the computation is first written as a circuit, a set of math constraints.

concepts.definition: An honest prover with a true statement can always convince the verifier.
A prover cannot convince the verifier of a false statement, except with negligible chance.
A proof delivered as a single message that anyone can verify without talking to the prover.
A computation expressed as math constraints so that it can be proven.

example.title: The colorblind friend
example.body: You hold two balls that look identical to a colorblind friend, one red and one green. Behind their back, they either swap the balls or not, and you say which. If you were guessing, you would fail half the time, so after many rounds they are convinced the balls differ. Yet they still do not know which ball is red.

modules.title: SNARKs vs STARKs
modules.summary: SNARKs and STARKs are the two main families of practical proof systems. They differ in setup, proof size, verification cost and security assumptions.
objectives: Explain what a trusted setup is and why it matters
Compare SNARK and STARK proof sizes and verification costs
Explain why STARKs are considered post-quantum secure

sections.heading: SNARKs
sections.body: SNARK stands for succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge. SNARK proofs are very small, often a few hundred bytes, and cheap to verify on-chain. Many common SNARKs rely on elliptic curve cryptography. Groth16 and PLONK are well-known SNARK systems.

sections.heading: Trusted setup
sections.body: Many SNARKs need a trusted setup, a ceremony that creates public parameters from secret randomness. If anyone kept that secret, sometimes called toxic waste, they could forge proofs. Ceremonies use many participants so that only one needs to be honest and delete their part. Groth16 needs a new setup per circuit, while PLONK uses one universal setup that many circuits can share.

sections.heading: STARKs
sections.body: STARK stands for scalable transparent argument of knowledge. Transparent means there is no trusted setup, since all randomness is public. STARKs rely only on hash functions. Their proofs are much larger than SNARK proofs, often tens of kilobytes or more, so they cost more to verify on-chain.

sections.heading: Quantum and trade-offs
sections.body: Elliptic curve cryptography could be broken by a large enough quantum computer. Hash-based STARKs are believed to resist quantum attacks, so they are considered post-quantum secure. Some systems combine both: they create a STARK, then wrap it in a small SNARK to make on-chain verification cheaper.

concepts.definition: Succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge, a proof system with very small proofs.
Scalable transparent argument of knowledge, a hash-based proof system with no trusted setup.
A ceremony that generates public parameters from secret randomness that must be destroyed.
Security that is believed to hold even against attackers with large quantum computers.

example.title: Zcash and its ceremony
example.body: Zcash launched in 2016 as one of the first major uses of zk-SNARKs for private payments. Before launch, it ran a trusted setup ceremony with several participants. The design meant forged coins would only be possible if every participant had kept their secret part.

modules.title: ZK rollups, zkEVMs and private transactions
modules.summary: ZK rollups use validity proofs to scale blockchains, zkEVMs make that work for Ethereum apps, and privacy systems use commitments and nullifiers to hide transfers.
objectives: Explain how a ZK rollup proves its state changes
Compare zkEVM types and the compatibility trade-off
Describe how commitments and nullifiers enable private transfers

sections.heading: ZK rollups
sections.body: A ZK rollup executes transactions off the main chain, then posts the transaction data and a validity proof to it. A contract on the main chain verifies the proof before accepting the new state. Unlike optimistic rollups, there is no challenge period to wait out, so withdrawals can finalize once the proof is verified.

sections.heading: zkEVM types
sections.body: A zkEVM proves the execution of Ethereum-style smart contracts. A widely used classification runs from Type 1, fully equivalent to Ethereum and slowest to prove, to Type 4, which compiles high-level code like Solidity into a different, proof-friendly machine. Lower types are more compatible with existing tools. Higher types prove faster but may break some contracts or tooling.

sections.heading: Private transactions
sections.body: Private payment systems hide amounts and parties using commitments, which are like sealed envelopes holding a value. To spend, a user proves in zero knowledge that they own an unspent commitment in the set. They also publish a nullifier, a unique tag derived from that note, without revealing which commitment it came from.

sections.heading: Why nullifiers matter
sections.body: If the same note is spent twice, it produces the same nullifier, so the second spend is rejected. This prevents double spending without linking the spend to the original deposit. The privacy set, meaning everyone who could have made the transfer, is what hides the user. A small set gives weak privacy.

concepts.definition: A proof that a batch of transactions was executed correctly according to the rules.
A system that produces proofs of correct execution for Ethereum-compatible smart contracts.
A cryptographic value that hides data while binding the creator to it.
A unique tag published when a private note is spent, used to block double spends.

example.title: Withdrawing from a ZK rollup
example.body: A user withdraws funds from a ZK rollup to Ethereum. The rollup includes the withdrawal in a batch, generates a validity proof, and posts it to its contract on Ethereum. Once the contract verifies the proof, the withdrawal can be completed without waiting through a fraud challenge window.

questions.prompt: What does a zero-knowledge proof let you do?
options: Encrypt a file so only one person can open it
Send tokens without paying any network fee
Prove a statement is true without revealing the secret
Recover a lost private key from its matching public address
questions.explanation: A zero-knowledge proof convinces a verifier that something is true while keeping the underlying secret hidden.

questions.prompt: In a zero-knowledge proof, who creates the proof?
options: The prover
The verifier
The validator
The oracle
questions.explanation: The prover knows the secret and creates the proof. The verifier only checks it.

questions.prompt: Why are zero-knowledge proofs useful for scaling blockchains?
options: They let every node skip storing any blockchain data at all
They make every transaction completely free
They remove the need for private keys
Checking a proof is much cheaper than redoing the work
questions.explanation: One party does the heavy computation and makes a proof. Everyone else verifies it cheaply instead of repeating the work.

questions.prompt: A site checks a proof that you are over 18. What does it learn?
options: Your exact birth date
Only that you are over 18
Your name and home address
Your ID document number
questions.explanation: The proof reveals only the statement being proven, that you are over 18, and nothing else.

questions.prompt: In blockchain systems, what often plays the role of the verifier?
options: A hardware wallet
A token holder
A smart contract
A block explorer
questions.explanation: A smart contract on-chain commonly checks proofs and accepts or rejects them automatically.

questions.prompt: Which property means a false statement cannot be proven, except with tiny chance?
options: Soundness
Completeness
Succinctness
Transparency
questions.explanation: Soundness guarantees a cheating prover cannot convince the verifier of something untrue.

questions.prompt: What does completeness guarantee?
options: The proof reveals nothing about the secret
The proof is smaller than the original data
No trusted setup is needed to create proofs
An honest prover with a true claim is accepted
questions.explanation: Completeness means true statements proven honestly will always be accepted by the verifier.

questions.prompt: Why do blockchains need non-interactive proofs?
options: Interactive proofs cannot be sound
A single proof is posted once and checked by many
Non-interactive proofs need no math or cryptography at all
Interactive proofs always leak the secret
questions.explanation: On a blockchain, nobody can hold a live conversation with the prover, so the proof must be one message anyone can check.

questions.prompt: In a proof system, what is a circuit?
options: A hardware chip that stores private keys
A loop of validators that sign each block
A computation written as math constraints
A network path between prover and verifier
questions.explanation: To prove a computation, it is first expressed as a circuit, a system of constraints the proof shows are satisfied.

questions.prompt: Many scaling rollups do not hide any data. What is a more precise name for their proofs?
options: Validity proofs
Fraud proofs
Proofs of stake
Proofs of work
questions.explanation: When the goal is proving correct execution rather than hiding data, the proof is better described as a validity proof.

questions.prompt: What does the T in STARK stand for, and what does it mean?
options: Trusted, it needs a setup ceremony
Transparent, it needs no trusted setup
Threshold, it needs several signers
Temporary, its proofs expire later
questions.explanation: STARKs are transparent: all randomness is public, so no trusted setup ceremony is required.

questions.prompt: In a trusted setup, what could someone do if they kept the secret randomness?
options: Read every private transaction's contents
Freeze any account that uses the system
Raise the fee required to verify a proof
Create fake proofs that verify as valid
questions.explanation: The leftover secret, often called toxic waste, would allow forging proofs that pass verification.

questions.prompt: Why are STARKs generally considered post-quantum secure?
options: They rely only on hash functions
They use larger elliptic curves
They run on quantum hardware
They require a trusted setup
questions.explanation: STARKs depend on hash functions, which are believed to resist quantum attacks, unlike elliptic curve assumptions.

questions.prompt: How do typical SNARK and STARK proof sizes compare?
options: They are always exactly the same size
SNARKs are much larger than STARKs
SNARKs are much smaller than STARKs
Size depends only on the blockchain used
questions.explanation: SNARK proofs are often a few hundred bytes, while STARK proofs are commonly tens of kilobytes or more.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between Groth16 and PLONK setups?
options: Groth16 has no setup at all while PLONK needs a new one per circuit
Both need a new ceremony for every single proof
Both share one universal setup used by all circuits
Groth16 needs a setup per circuit while PLONK's is universal
questions.explanation: Groth16 requires a circuit-specific ceremony, while PLONK uses one universal setup that many circuits can reuse.

questions.prompt: Why can ZK rollup withdrawals finalize without a long challenge period?
options: A trusted operator approves each withdrawal manually
A validity proof shows the new state is correct
Withdrawals skip the main chain entirely
Fraud is impossible because data is never posted
questions.explanation: The main-chain contract verifies a validity proof before accepting the state, so there is nothing to wait to challenge.

questions.prompt: Compared with a Type 4 zkEVM, what is true of a Type 1 zkEVM?
options: It is more Ethereum-compatible but slower to prove
It proves faster but breaks more existing contracts
It compiles Solidity into a different virtual machine
It needs no proofs because it trusts the sequencer
questions.explanation: Type 1 aims for full Ethereum equivalence, which maximizes compatibility at the cost of slower proving.

questions.prompt: In a private payment system, what stops the same note being spent twice?
options: The sender's address is checked against a list
A trusted server records every private balance
Each spend publishes a unique nullifier
Notes expire after one block has passed
questions.explanation: Spending a note reveals its nullifier. A second spend would repeat it and be rejected, without revealing which note it was.

questions.prompt: Why does a small privacy set weaken a private transaction system?
options: It makes the proofs too large to verify
It forces users to reveal their nullifiers
It requires a new trusted setup each time
Fewer possible senders makes each easier to guess
questions.explanation: Privacy comes from hiding among others. If few people use the system, linking a transfer to a user becomes much easier.

questions.prompt: Why might a project wrap a STARK proof inside a SNARK?
options: To add a trusted setup that improves the privacy of the proof
To get a small proof that is cheap to verify on-chain
To make the system fully post-quantum secure
To let the verifier learn the prover's secret
questions.explanation: The STARK does the heavy proving with no trusted setup, and the SNARK wrapper shrinks it so on-chain verification costs less.
